newsitem.title: CANADA: Coors/Molson agree to temporary truce in beer war.
newsitem.headline: Coors/Molson agree to temporary truce in beer war.

text.p: Canada's biggest brewer, Molson Breweries, and U.S. beermaker Adolph Coors Co. reached a temporary truce on Thursday in their battle over Molson's licensing rights to Coors' top-selling beers in Canada.
Molson and Coors agreed that Molson would continue to brew and sell Coors Light, Canada's dominant light beer, and Original Coors, at least through June 30, 1997.

But there is no guarantee that Thursday's agreement will lead to a long-term deal with the Colorado brewer, which also posted higher third-quarter profits Thursday, citing a special royalty payment from Molson Breweries.
"Do not read anything into this interim agreement about Coors' longterm plans in Canada," Coors' spokesman Jon Goldman said.
"We entered this agreement ... to ensure there is ongoing availability of our product in Canada while we explore our options," Goldman said.

He said Coors could export beer to Canada, contract it out, sell a participation interest or find a joint venture partner. These are options Coors could execute on their own, with Molson or with some other brewer, he said.
"The one thing we can say with certainty, is that any new agreement will not be a licensing arrangement and we will keep control of our brands in Canada," he said.
Analysts speculated that Coors could establish a Canadian subsidiary, noting that Hamilton, Ontario based Lakeport Brewery is for sale. Lakeport is a unit of Canadian soft drink bottler Cott Corp.
Coors could also negotiate with Molson's arch rival, Labatt Brewing Co., a unit of Belgian brewing giant Interbrew S.A, analysts said.
"We are following the developments closely. It is of interest because it is a sizable piece of business, but it's too early to speculate," said Labatt spokesman Bob Chant.

Meanwhile, Thursday's interim deal came two weeks after an arbitration panel tore up Molson's contract for Coors beer in Canada. The Oct. 18 ruling said Molson breached its licensing deal by allowing Miller Brewing Co., a unit of Philip Morris Cos. Inc., to buy a 20 percent stake without Coors' consent in 1993.
Molson Breweries is also owned 40 percent each by Toronto-based Molson Cos. Ltd. and Australia's Foster's Brewing Group Ltd..
The panel ordered Molson to pay damages to Coors that could total tens of millions of dollars. The exact amount will be determined early in 1997.

"It's an ongoing saga. This (interim deal) is a stop-gap and it's encouraging, but we want to see a long-term agreement signed," said Mike Palmer, an analyst with Toronto-based brokerage Loewen, Ondaatje, McCutcheon Ltd.
Coors said its net income for the 13 weeks ended Sept. 29 rose to $18.7 million, or 49 cents a share, from $16.5 million, or 43 cents a share.
The increase was due mainly to an after-tax credit of $4.1 million, or 11 cents a share, related to a Molson payment of $4.8 million for underpaid royalties resulting from the panel's ruling.
Under the interim agreement, Coors said it it will receive at least an additional $10 million of pretax income from Molson during the nine-month period ending in June 1997.
The arrangement will knock about C$15 million ($11 million) from Molson Breweries' bottom line, said spokesman Barry Joslin.
"It doesn't ensure that we will reach a long-term agreement ... but if we can come to a meeting of minds that would be everybody's preference," Joslin said.
Molson can ill afford to lose a profitable brand as it battles Labatt in a domestic beer market that has been flat for several years, analysts said.

Coors brands produced by Molson -- Coors Light and Original Coors -- account for 8 percent of its sales volume. Coors Light is the top-selling light beer in Canada, commanding a 5 to 5.5 percent share of the beer market.

"Coors is being presented with other options so there is no guarantee that they can do a long-term deal. But as long as everyone acts in a business-like fashion, I think a deal is in the best interests of both parties," said Palmer, the analyst.
Meanwhile, both companies will face an arbitration panel in early 1997 to haggle over the damages owed to Coors.
The Oct. 18 ruling ordered Molson to pay Coors the profit it made on selling Coors' brands since April 2, 1993, when Miller Brewing acquired its stake.
Molson said the amount is hard to estimate, but analysts said the damages could be in the tens of millions of dollars.
"Coors obviously will take the position that they want as much money as possible, and we'll take the position that a reasonable share of the profits is a lower number," Joslin said.
Molson Cos' class A stock gained C$0.10 ($0.07) to C$20.20 ($15) on the Toronto Stock Exchange, but remained well off its year high of C$25.125 ($18.80).
On Nasdaq, Coors' stock climbed 0.75 to 19.25.
